titleArabic: الشيخ الأكبر محيي الدين ابن عربي

verses.ar:
Name and title: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Muhammad Ibn Arabi al-Ta'i al-Hatimi, known as Muhyiddin (Reviver of the Religion) and al-Shaykh al-Akbar (the Greatest Shaykh).
Born: Ramadan 560 AH (1165 CE), Murcia, al-Andalus. The sources differ on the day (17th or 27th).
Died: 22 Rabi al-Thani 638 AH (16 November 1240 CE), Damascus, where his tomb stands.
Teachers: al-Uryani, his first teacher, and many scholars and saints in al-Andalus and North Africa, among them Fatima bint Ibn al-Muthanna of Seville.
Students: Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, his stepson and chief interpreter, and Ismail ibn Sawdakin.
Works: some 700 books, treatises and poems, of which about 400 survive, among them al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya (begun in Mecca, finished about 635 AH), Fusus al-Hikam (completed in Damascus about 627–628 AH) and the poems Tarjuman al-Ashwaq.

Shaykh Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi (QS) was born in Murcia in 1165 and grew up in Seville. He studied the Qur'an and the sacred law, and as a young man a voice called to him in the midst of a gathering of friends, “O Muhammad, it was not for this that you were created”. He withdrew into retreat in a cemetery, and there he received his great vision, in which he met Jesus, Moses and Muhammad ﷺ and was instructed by them; from that vision his path began. He sat with the saints of al-Andalus, among them Fatima of Seville, and his first teacher was al-Uryani. In 1200 he left Spain and never returned, travelling by Cairo and Jerusalem to Mecca, where he performed the pilgrimage in 1202 and began the Futuhat al-Makkiyya. He visited Baghdad, Konya and Aleppo, and in 1223 settled in Damascus, where he taught kings and seekers alike until he passed away on 22 Rabi al-Thani 638 AH (16 November 1240). His tomb is in Damascus, and his urs is kept on that day.

Ibn Arabi wrote some 700 works, about 400 of which survive, on the knowledge of Allah, the inner reality of the Prophet ﷺ, the stations of the saints and the unseen. In the Futuhat al-Makkiyya, begun in Mecca, he shows the whole of the religion, its acts of worship and the spiritual states that grow from them, as a path to knowing Allah; the Fusus al-Hikam takes each prophet as a wisdom of the Divine Names. His followers called him al-Shaykh al-Akbar, the Greatest Shaykh, and his stepson Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi (QS) began the work of explaining and passing on his teachings. For the people of the path he stands among the great knowers of Allah and the masters of the secrets of the heart, and his books are read in the circles of the Sufis, under the guidance of a shaykh, as a key to the realities behind the sacred law, which he held to be the root of every station.
